content_html:
Cusco, the historic capital of the Inca Empire, is full of mysteries and symbolism in its streets and squares. Something that draws the attention of locals and tourists is the presence of several streets with the number "seven" in his name. This peculiarity is no coincidence, since the number seven had a sacred meaning for the Incas, related to their worldview and the organization of their world.

Below, we will explore some of the most famous streets with "seven" in their name and the possible origin of this tradition.

1. Siete Culebras Street

Located between the church of San Antonio Abad and the old Monastery of the Nazarenas, this pedestrian street is famous for the 14 snakes carved into its stone walls, seven on each side. formerly called Amaru Ccata (in Quechua: "snake"), its current name derives from these serpentine representations.

2. Seven Little Angels Street

Located in the San Blas neighborhood, this street gets its name from a painting on the ceiling of an old house that showed seven little angels. The image was commissioned by Blas de Bobadilla, and the street is located near Carmen Alto Street, about 15 minutes from Cusco's Plaza de Armas.

3. Seven Little Devils Street

Also in the San Blas neighborhood, this street owes its name to an old painting that represented seven imps. Although the original painting no longer exists, the name persists, adding a touch of mystery to the place.

4. Seven Windows Street

Located in the historic center of Cusco, near the Plazoleta de San Agustín, this street takes its name from an old construction that had seven windows on its facade.

5. Calle Siete Cuartones

Near Plaza San Francisco, this street is called that because, in colonial times, it was divided into seven sections or "cuartones". Furthermore, it is mentioned that its name refers to seven stone stringers aligned over the Saphy River.

6. Calle Siete Mascarones

This street gets its name from the presence of seven masks stone carvings that adorned one of the colonial houses in the area.

7. Calle Siete Borreguitos

This street used to be frequented by people walking with their livestock and packages, adding to the picturesque atmosphere of the place.

Why so many streets with 7?

The presence of the number seven in these streets it has generated various interpretations. Some believe that it has a character cabalistic introduced during the colony, while others suggest that its use dates back to times before the Incas, given that the number seven has a symbolic meaning in many cultures around the world.

Exploring these streets offers a unique insight into Cusco's rich history and culture, allowing visitors to immerse themselves in the traditions and legends that have shaped the city over the centuries.
